title: How Tibo keeps customers forever: filter requests, raise prices, build moats
summary: Tibo argues retention is a high-margin system that compounds, unlike acquisition, which resets every month. He gives five levers: filter feature requests instead of complying, build systems, raise prices to change who your customer is, make customization a moat, and tie customers' own success to your product.

principles.text: Retention is built once and compounds; acquisition is an expensive sprint you repeat forever.
principles.quote: Retention is different. It's a system you build once. High margin, compounds instead of resetting every month, and it's what actually stacks MRR and builds enterprise value over time.

principles.text: Filter feature requests rather than complying; protect your differentiated workflow and higher-tier value.
principles.quote: Your job as a founder isn't to comply. It's to filter.

principles.text: Saying no to requests that erase your product's difference is why people choose you (Revid skips micro-control for full video generation).
principles.quote: We get a lot of requests asking for more manual control. If we said yes to all of them, we'd become exactly like every other AI video tool out there.

principles.text: Fix categories of problems with systems, not one-off patches, so revenue compounds.
principles.quote: When you solve a user's problem, ask if you just patched one instance or built something that prevents the whole category of problems.

principles.text: Raising prices lowers churn because higher-paying customers have skin in the game and make the product work.
principles.quote: At Tweet Hunter, we started at $9/month. Then we raised it, eventually landing at $49/month. The expected outcome was more churn. The actual outcome was the opposite.

principles.text: Customization and tying users' own results to your product make leaving costly.
principles.quote: The more a user configures a product around their exact workflow, the harder it becomes for them to leave.
